title: Knock (1879)
hook: a silent apparition in the rain in an Irish village

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatima, simply: children asked to pray every day and turn back to God. Your line was pray and repent. What did you turn around from, even for an hour? Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

It's a wet evening in a small village in the west of Ireland, and it's raining hard. A woman walking past the parish church stops. She sees figures, she'll later say, at the gable wall, standing in a soft light, a little above the grass. She runs for others. Neighbors come, then more neighbors, old people and children. They stand in the downpour and look, and kneel, and someone starts the rosary. The figures don't move toward them. Nobody calls out to the crowd, nobody asks for anything, nobody gives a message. People stay a long time, soaked, praying, watching. And then it's over. Today's word is the village where the vision said nothing at all.
screen: `RAIN ON A VILLAGE CHURCH.` → `FIGURES AT THE GABLE WALL.` → `NOBODY SAYS A WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the silence itself. Lourdes had a lady who spoke to Bernadette; Fatima had requests for the children. At Knock, by the witnesses' accounts, no one spoke at all. Not Mary, not anyone. For a Church that has heard so many words, that's a striking thing to keep. Second, who was there. The witnesses described Mary, crowned, her hands raised and her eyes lifted, as if in prayer. Beside her, Joseph, his head bowed toward her. On her other side, a figure they took to be John the Evangelist, dressed like a bishop and holding an open book. And in the middle, an altar, with a cross and a lamb standing on it. Third, the lamb. The Book of the Apocalypse, the one John is said to have written, has this scene. In the Douay-Rheims, John sees in heaven "a Lamb standing as it were slain." For Christians, the Lamb is Christ: wounded, and alive. At Knock, the witnesses placed that altar and its lamb at the center. Some readers see the whole vision as a picture of the Mass, with Mary, Joseph and John gathered around it, saying nothing, because the one in the middle is the point. Fourth, why silence speaks. Knock was a poor village in a country that had known famine and hard years. What came was not a lecture or a warning. It was company, in the rain. The prophet Habacuc has a line for it: "But the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him." At Knock, the earth did.
screen: `NO ONE SPOKE.` · `MARY, JOSEPH, JOHN.` · `A LAMB ON THE ALTAR.` · `SILENCE AS COMPANY.` · then, large: `LET ALL THE EARTH KEEP SILENCE BEFORE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silence in prayer. Settle, and breathe. Today, no words, not even inside. If a thought starts talking, let it trail off, the way a conversation stops when someone points at the sky. Bring to mind the people at the gable wall, kneeling in the rain, watching. You don't have to see anything. Just be someone who stays. If you pray, let this be prayer without a single word in it. If you don't, let it be two minutes of honest quiet. The bell holds the time.
Knock. The Irish village where, by the witnesses' accounts, Mary, Joseph and John stood beside an altar with a lamb, in the rain, and not one word was spoken. Today's word.

Your line: the silent apparition. Today, leave one gap unfilled: a pause in a conversation, a wait in line, a drive without the radio, and let it stay quiet. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to the shrine at Knock in County Mayo, Ireland, where the gable wall of the old parish church is kept as a chapel; pilgrims pray the rosary there and come for Mass and confession.

fork.setup: you're kneeling in the rain at the church wall. the figures are right there. you wait for the lady to speak. what does she say?

a request to build a chapel here.
fork.reveal: nothing. by the witnesses' accounts the vision was silent. the lamb on the altar stood at the center, and the people stayed and prayed.

original.note: Latin: Lamb of God, sung at Mass before communion; the lamb stood at the center of the vision at Knock.

trapdoor: what you thought: an apparition is heaven sending a message.
what it means: at Knock, no one spoke. Mary, Joseph and John stood beside a lamb on an altar while villagers prayed in the rain.
what a scholar hears: Apocalypse 5:6, the Lamb standing as it were slain, at the center of a silent tableau some readers take as a picture of the Mass.

notes: Editor: the hook now reports the figures through the witness; cut 'every figure turns toward that altar' (the accounts have Mary's eyes raised) here and in the fork and trapdoor; new carry, since 'keep company without fixing' repeated day 1333's carry.

No date or number of witnesses is given in the voice (the title keeps the index's '1879'). Details from the witnesses' depositions (Mary crowned, hands raised, eyes lifted; Joseph bowed toward her; a figure taken to be John the Evangelist in bishop's vestments with an open book; an altar with a cross and a lamb; angels are also reported and are omitted): confirm.
'A woman walking past the parish church' simplifies the accounts (Mary McLoughlin, the priest's housekeeper, and Mary Byrne are usually named as the first). Confirm acceptable without names.
'Lourdes had a lady who spoke; Fatima had requests' compares apparitions within the Catholic tradition, not traditions; confirm the framing.
'The one John is said to have written' attributes the Apocalypse's authorship as tradition. Confirm.
'Some readers see the whole vision as a picture of the Mass': confirm attribution.
'A poor village in a country that had known famine and hard years': general history without dates; confirm the framing is careful.
Douay-Rheims wording of Apocalypse 5:6 and Habacuc 2:20: confirm.
